findings.description: derivePassword() builds the Jasypt BasicTextEncryptor (PBEWithMD5AndDES) password as reverse(busId + version) — both plaintext, not-null columns stored in the same `sec` row. For the JWT key the inputs are the compile-time constants JWT_BUS_NAME="jot" and JWT_VERSION="v1" (SecurityConstants.java:58-59), making the password the fixed string "1vtoj" in every environment. Anyone who gains read access to the database (SQL injection anywhere in the app, a leaked backup/dump, read-replica or support SELECT access) decrypts the HMAC signing key and can forge a JWT for any user and any role including ROLE_ADMIN, fully bypassing authentication. @Audited additionally copies every encrypted value into the Envers sec_aud history table, widening the leak surface and making the key impossible to scrub.
findings.title: JWT signing key decryptable by anyone with read access to the sec table — Jasypt password derived from plaintext columns of the same row
findings.verification: Confirm the sec/sec_aud tables exist via the Flyway migrations and that no additional external encryption (e.g. pgcrypto, disk-level with column access control) applies; decrypt a sample row with BasicTextEncryptor and password "1vtoj" to demonstrate.

findings.description: Both JwtSecretService and JwtConfiguration cache the Secret in a volatile field set once and never invalidated, and the lookup they use (SecretService.fetchSecret -> SecretRepository.findOneByVersionAndBusId) ignores EntityStatus entirely. After a key compromise, marking the row INACTIVE changes nothing: running instances keep signing and verifying with the cached key, and even restarted instances fetch and honor the INACTIVE row. Because Secret's columns are updatable=false, (version,busId) is unique, and JWT_VERSION is a constant, there is no operational path to replace the key — tokens forged with a stolen key remain valid indefinitely until a code change and full redeploy.
findings.title: JWT secret cannot be revoked or rotated: status flag ignored and key cached per-instance forever
findings.verification: Confirm there is no admin endpoint or scheduled job that evicts JwtConfiguration.secret / JwtSecretService.secret or re-reads the row; confirm EntityStatus on the sec row is consulted nowhere on the JWT path.

findings.description: The method caches the latest ACTIVE Secret per busId in an in-memory ConcurrentHashMap that is never evicted, so deactivating a secret or inserting a newer active one never takes effect on a running instance, and in the multi-instance deployment different instances can serve different "latest" secrets after a rotation, each rejecting material signed by the other. No caller exists in src/main/java today, so the defect is latent, but any future consumer silently inherits broken revocation and rotation semantics.
findings.title: fetchLatestActiveSecretAsBytes caches secrets in a per-JVM map with no TTL or invalidation
findings.verification: Grep the full tree (including tests and other modules) for callers of fetchLatestActiveSecretAsBytes; if a consumer exists, severity rises to medium.

findings.description: targetsLoopback passes any datasource host that resolves to loopback, link-local, or RFC 1918 private space — the last of which is where most cloud production databases sit. If app.bootstrap.jwt-secret.enabled=true is copied into a production configuration and the database has no secret row yet, the runner seeds the JWT signing key through this dev-only path instead of failing the boot as the guard intends. The seeded value is SecureRandom so direct impact is limited to the weak at-rest storage of finding 1; the javadoc acknowledges the gap as a deliberate tradeoff, leaving the enabled flag as the only effective gate against the exact misconfiguration the guard was added for.
findings.title: Bootstrap runner's local-only guard accepts RFC 1918 hosts, i.e. most production VPC databases
findings.verification: Check prod/uat deployment configs and secret stores to confirm app.bootstrap.jwt-secret.enabled is not set there, and whether the production database host resolves to RFC 1918 space.
